explanation: Write preorder values with explicit null markers and token separators. Decoding consumes one token per recursive position. The string fully specifies structure and values, even in a separate process.
timeComplexity: O(n squared) conservative serialization bound if concatenations copy strings: a skew tree repeatedly concatenates growing descendant encodings. Engines may use ropes to avoid these copies. Tokenizing and decoding take O(n) time for fixed-width values.
spaceComplexity: O(n + h) serialization/token space and recursion, plus the decoded tree. Serialization buffers, decoded tokens, and the new tree are linear in n; recursion uses h frames.
attribution: Original repository-authored Blind75 JavaScript algorithm, promoted from the validated correct fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: Preorder emits each root before its two child encodings, including an explicit null token for every missing child. A decoder consumes exactly one token to distinguish empty from nonempty, then recursively consumes the required children. Structural induction proves this is a unique inverse and needs no encoder process state.
walkthrough: For [6,null,9,7], preorder tokens are 6,#,9,7,#,#,#. The first # gives node 6 no left child; the remaining tokens create right child 9 with left child 7. Decoding the string reconstructs the same level-order tree [6,null,9,7]. The example represents Serialize followed by Deserialize independently; expected is the rebuilt tree in level order, with fresh-node identity and input preservation checked separately.
edgeCases: A null tree still needs an explicit null encoding.
Negative and multidigit values require token separators.
Encoding and decoding run in separate processes.
